Background
I’m originally from Harbour Grace, Newfoundland. My academic journey spans:
BSc (Joint Hons) Applied Math & Physics — Research in numerical methods for adaptive mesh generation under Dr. Ronald Haynes
MSc Mathematics — Theoretical research on black hole geometry under Dr. Hari Kunduri
BEd Intermediate/Secondary Education — Teaching internship at Prince of Wales Collegiate, St. John’s
My professional experience includes:
- Post-secondary mathematics instructor at College of the North Atlantic (2019–2021)
- Health Information Specialist at Health PEI (statistical analysis and data visualization)
- Learning Manager of Mathematics and Physics at Holland College (2022–present)
Service & Community
Faculty Representative, Holland College Accessibility and Inclusion Advisory Council
Member, City of Charlottetown Affordable Housing Advisory Board
Trustee, Public Schools Branch (PEI) — Chair, Finance & Audit Committee
Personal



In my spare time, I enjoy outdoor activities — from relaxing beach trips to day-long hiking expeditions. Growing up in Newfoundland gave me ample opportunity to explore nature, a passion I continue on beautiful Prince Edward Island. I live in Charlottetown with my wife and our six pets (2 dogs and 4 cats).

articles.title: Academic Publications
articles.contents:
MSc (Mathematics) Thesis
Title:
Constructing Static Black Hole‑Soliton Spacetimes
Supervisor:
Dr. Hari Kunduri
Year:
2019
Abstract:
This work constructs new static solutions of five‑dimensional vacuum general relativity describing asymptotically flat black hole‑soliton spacetimes. Using Weyl solutions, explicit metrics are built and studied. The thesis then generalizes to non‑vanishing Maxwell fields, obtaining static, electrically charged black hole‑soliton spacetimes. A solution‑generating technique involving boosts and dualities is employed.
Link
BSc (Applied Mathematics and Physics Honours) Thesis
Title: Adaptive Mesh Methods and a Schwarz Algorithm Implementation of a Smoothed Mesh Generating Function
Supervisor: Dr. Ronald Haynes
Year: 2015
Abstract:
Employing an adaptive mesh for solving PDEs improves accuracy in regions of complex behaviour. This thesis implements a classic Schwarz algorithm for a monitor function, studies convergence and accuracy, and extends to domain decomposition for parallelization. Numerical simulations demonstrate successful application of smoothed mesh techniques.
